## Six clicks that could be two groups or three

Equal clicks never tell you where a bar starts. Play a stream of identical
ticks and your listener will settle on some grouping, but it's theirs, not
yours, and it can flip while they're listening. Something has to recur and
carry more weight. That's all an accent is, and it moves nothing at all in
time.

*Meter* is the recurring pattern of strong and weak beats through which you
hear a bar. In a stream of eighth notes, an accent every two subdivisions
points at quarter-note beats; an accent every three points at dotted-quarter
beats. Six eighths is the smallest span that shows both. In 3/4 they fall as
three groups of two. In 6/8 they fall as two groups of three. Both versions
occupy three quarter-note beats, and both hold the same six onsets in the same
six places.

So the program keeps those six durations locked and changes nothing but the
amplitude cycle. Follow the strong clicks first. Then hear how the weak ones
arrange themselves around what you found.

## One duration array, three accent cycles

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 92

define :play_meter do |durations, accents, expected|
  raise "bar length mismatch" unless durations.sum == expected
  durations.each_with_index do |duration, index|
    sample :elec_tick, amp: accents[index % accents.length]
    sleep duration
  end
  sleep 1
end

eighths = [0.5] * 6
play_meter eighths, [1.2, 0.55], 3.0
play_meter eighths, [1.2, 0.55, 0.55], 3.0
play_meter eighths, [0.8], 3.0
```

Same sample, same six eighth-note sleeps, same three-beat total, three times
over. The first profile accents every other eighth and pushes you toward three
quarter-note groups. The second accents every third eighth and pushes toward
two dotted-quarter groups. The third takes the evidence away and leaves you a
flat stream. Here's the one to pay attention to: on that third pass, which
grouping do you hear, and where do you think it came from?

## Narrow the gap between strong and weak

1. Drop the strongest amplitude from `1.2` to `0.9`. As strong and weak
   converge, the meter gets harder to pin down, and the six onsets haven't
   budged a millisecond.

2. Restore the original and rewrite the 6/8 profile as `[1.2, 0.5, 0.5, 0.9,
   0.5, 0.5]`. That secondary accent on the fourth eighth marks the second half
   of the bar while the first half keeps the strongest weight. You now have
   two levels of grouping in one array.

3. Restore the profiles and delete one eighth from the duration array, leaving
   the assertion in place. Read the error in the log and connect it to the half
   beat missing from a bar that promised three.

## An accent array is a weight function

The accent array repeats. For each event, `index % accents.length` picks a
level out of that cycle, so a two-value array gives you strong-weak and a
three-value array gives you strong-weak-weak. Run either over the same
eighth-note stream and your ear draws its boundaries in different places.

Validation covers a different failure entirely. `durations.sum == expected`
proves the bar occupies the promised amount of musical time. It has no opinion
about how anyone groups that time. Both 3/4 and 6/8 come to three quarter-note
beats here, so both sail past the same assertion while partitioning the span
differently. Keep that split clear and you'll debug rhythm faster: the log
catches arithmetic, and only playback catches grouping. A bar can total
correctly and still point its weight at the wrong place, and a convincing
accent pattern can be cut short by one missing event.

Amplitude is one source of accent, and it's the right one for this comparison
because a stronger attack grabs attention while pitch, timbre and duration hold
still. Music makes weight in plenty of other ways: a lower pitch, a different
drum, a longer note, a change of harmony. Those cues usually reinforce each
other in real music. They also add colour that makes the underlying pattern
harder to isolate, which is why this program uses one tick and one number.

Don't skip past the unaccented pass. It's there to show you that meter isn't
printed into equal subdivisions. You'll often keep hearing whichever grouping
came before it, running on memory, or you'll impose a new one for no reason you
can name. Play the three profiles in a different order and watch that neutral
stream change character without changing a single sample.

[Lesson 14](14-rests-dots-ties.qmd) adds rests and sustained events while leaving this duration
arithmetic intact. A bar keeps occupying its time when one position has no
attack, and a note can cross a boundary without being struck again.

## Three profiles, one assertion

Write one six-eighth duration array and three named accent profiles: 3/4, 6/8,
and an even control. Make them selectable by editing a single symbol, and put
all three behind one assertion that demands three quarter-note beats.

Audition them in Sonic Pi 5 without touching the sample or the tempo. Find the
one accent position that most cleanly separates three groups of two from two
groups of three, then weaken that accent and listen again. What you'll have
demonstrated is both layers at once: one shared numerical span, and audible
groupings that disagree about it.
